subtitle: Ground-Level Air Quality Intelligence
summary: A workflow that combines Sentinel-5P satellite data with ERA5 meteorology to map ground-level NO₂, O₃, PM10 and PM2.5 over Lombardy.
heroText: From satellite columns to ground-level concentrations of NO₂, O₃, PM10 and PM2.5 over Lombardy, ready for hourly prediction with Sentinel-4.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: The product turns satellite column measurements into daily air-quality maps at the surface, for 1,244 points covering the whole region, and is built to move to hourly prediction when Sentinel-4 becomes operational. It estimates ground-level concentrations of four pollutants by linking satellite observations, meteorology and reference air-quality data.

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Satellites see a column, people breathe at ground level
story.text: Satellites measure the atmosphere as a vertical column, while health and policy decisions depend on what people breathe at ground level. Ground stations measure that directly, but they are sparse and unevenly distributed.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Satellite, weather and reference data
story.text: Sentinel-5P (TROPOMI) tropospheric NO₂, O₃, SO₂, HCHO and UV aerosol index, ERA5 meteorology, CAMS and ARPA Lombardia reference maps, plus elevation, emissions and land use.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: One regression per pollutant and target
story.text: For each pollutant, one satellite indicator is smoothed over the previous days and combined with five meteorological variables in a multiple regression. The same structure is applied to the CAMS and ARPA references, giving eight models.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Sentinel-5P
items.text: Tropospheric NO₂, O₃, SO₂, HCHO and UV aerosol index, from the Copernicus Data Space.

items.name: ERA5
items.text: Temperature, wind, boundary layer height, precipitation and solar radiation.

items.name: CAMS and ARPA Lombardia
items.text: CAMS modelled air quality and the ARPA 1 × 1 km assimilated maps, used as reference targets.

items.name: Static layers
items.text: Elevation (DEM), emission maps and land use.

deliverables: Daily maps of estimated NO₂, O₃, PM10 and PM2.5 concentrations for 2025, with monthly and yearly summaries.
Residual maps that show where the estimate departs from the reference.
Coverage and quality layers that show where and when an estimate is available and how reliable it is.

methods.title: From raw data to the final product
text: Satellite, meteorological and reference data are downloaded for the same period with a single script, reprojected and resampled to a 500 m grid, and sampled at the 1,244 points. For each pollutant, one satellite indicator is selected, smoothed over the previous days, and combined with five meteorological variables in a multiple regression. The models are checked with a time-based validation and then re-fitted on the full year to produce the maps.

The choice of satellite indicators comes from a correlation analysis. NO₂ is the clearest signal, ozone moves in the opposite direction to NO₂, and particulate matter is the hardest to capture from space.

subtitle: Urban Growth & Farmland Monitoring
summary: Land-cover change from Sentinel-2 to track urban growth and farmland loss around Iasi, Romania for economic activity monitoring and urban planning.
heroText: Land-cover change from Sentinel-2 to track urban growth and farmland loss around Iasi, Romania.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: Cities grow onto farmland, and the loss is slow, spread out and easy to miss. This project measures it with public satellite images, so the answer is objective and can be repeated every year. It asks how much the built-up area has grown, how much farmland was lost and what it became, and whether farmland at risk can be spotted before construction starts.

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Farmland loss is slow and easy to miss
story.text: Urban growth eats into farmland gradually and across many small places. The project needs an objective, repeatable measure of how much was lost and what it became.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Summer composites from Sentinel-2
story.text: June to August composites at 10 m through Google Earth Engine, with cloudy scenes excluded and remaining clouds, shadows and cirrus masked. Ten spectral indices for vegetation, built-up surfaces, bare soil and water.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: Classify each year, then compare
story.text: Threshold rules assign each pixel to a land-cover class. Area per class is tracked over time, a transition matrix compares the first and last year, and index differences show how strong the change is.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Sentinel-2 Level-2A
items.text: Surface reflectance at 10 m through Google Earth Engine. June to August composites, scenes over 20% cloud excluded, and remaining clouds, shadows and cirrus masked with the SCL band.

items.name: Reference data
items.text: None yet. Points from high-resolution images or official land-use data are planned for a supervised classifier.

deliverables: Tables as CSV and charts as PNG.
An interactive map with one layer per year.
Optional GeoTIFF exports to Google Drive.

methods.title: From raw data to the final product
text: The study area is the city of Iasi and the surrounding farmland and periurban area, defined as a configurable rectangle. The official county boundary can be used instead.

steps.title: 1. Acquire and composite images
steps.text: For each year, summer scenes are filtered and masked, then combined into a median image that is more robust than a single scene.

steps.title: 2. Compute ten spectral indices
steps.text: NDVI, SAVI, MSAVI2, EVI and LAI for vegetation, NDBI and IBI for built-up surfaces, BSI for bare soil, and NDWI and MNDWI for water.

steps.title: 3. Classify land cover
steps.text: Threshold rules assign each pixel to water, agriculture and vegetation, urban, bare soil or unclassified, in that order of priority.

steps.title: 4. Detect change
steps.text: Area per class is tracked over time, a transition matrix compares the first and last year, and index differences show how strong the change is.

steps.title: 5. Export results
steps.text: Tables as CSV, charts as PNG, an interactive map with one layer per year, and optional GeoTIFF exports to Google Drive.

subtitle: Urban Green Cover Mapping
summary: A QGIS-based machine-learning workflow for hierarchical urban green-cover mapping from Sentinel-2 data.
heroText: Sentinel-2 imagery, terrain predictors and multi-source reference labels turned into a four-class green-cover map with probability, uncertainty and confidence.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: Urban green cover supports climate adaptation, biodiversity, environmental quality and planning. Green Detector is a QGIS plugin that builds a 10 m Sentinel-2 predictor stack, trains a hierarchical classifier that first separates green from non-green surfaces and then tells agricultural, forest and shrub-and-herbaceous vegetation apart, and delivers a four-class map together with probability, uncertainty and confidence layers.

meta.Area: Metropolitan City of Reggio Calabria, Italy
meta.Output: QGIS plugin, four-class map and confidence

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Reproducible green mapping with uncertainty
story.text: Mapping urban green cover with satellites is well established, but operational workflows often lack reproducibility, an assessment of uncertainty, and a direct link to geographic information systems.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Sentinel-2, terrain and reference labels
story.text: A 10 m Sentinel-2 predictor stack with elevation and slope, trained on vegetation, bare-soil, building, road and water references over 97 municipalities with a sharp gradient from the coast to the mountains.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: A hierarchical classifier
story.text: First separate green from non-green surfaces, then tell vegetation types apart. Filtering the vegetation-type result with the green decision removes buildings and roads labelled as vegetation, and extra layers show where a prediction is weakly supported.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Sentinel-2 Level-2A
items.text: Two adjacent tiles from the same acquisition of 4 June 2025. Bands B02, B03, B04 and B08 at their native 10 m; B11 and B12 resampled from 20 m to 10 m. The scene classification layer supplies the water reference.

items.name: Digital elevation model
items.text: 10 m DEM aligned to the Sentinel-2 grid. Slope is computed in degrees with the Zevenbergen-Thorne algorithm.

items.name: Administrative boundary
items.text: Official ISTAT boundary of the Metropolitan City, rasterized on the 10 m grid: 31,819,826 pixels.

items.name: Vegetation references
items.text: Polygons for agricultural vegetation (903), forest vegetation (229) and shrub and herbaceous vegetation (331), plus 6,643 auxiliary green labels derived with AI.

items.name: Non-green references
items.text: Bare-soil polygons (1,722), urban non-green polygons (120), OpenStreetMap building footprints (163,483), buffered road polygons (33,659) and water pixels from the scene classification layer.

deliverables: Binary green and non-green classification, with a green-cover probability and a binary uncertainty layer.
Three-class vegetation-type map, with class probabilities, maximum class probability and normalised predictive entropy.
Final four-class map: non-green, agricultural, forest, and shrub and herbaceous vegetation.
Hierarchical confidence layer that combines the support of both models.

methods.title: From raw data to the final product
text: The hierarchy matters because a model trained only on vegetation classes labels every pixel as some kind of vegetation, buildings and roads included. Filtering the vegetation-type result with the green/non-green decision removes that error. The extra layers show where a prediction is weakly supported, so the class map is not read as more certain than it is.

Green Detector is organized in tabs that match the processing modules: data preparation, feature construction, dataset generation, model training, prediction, post-processing, quality control and transferability. Each stage can be run and checked on its own, and trained models and scaling settings are stored apart from the interface. The finished workflow was also applied, without retraining, to Villa Borghese, a historic urban park of about 135 ha in Rome, to test how well it transfers to a very different landscape.

subtitle: Urban Heat & Resilience Assessment
summary: A 36-month satellite assessment of relative surface heat, land-cover dynamics and intervention opportunities in Reggio Calabria.
heroText: Six complementary indicators from monthly Sentinel-2 composites show where relative heat pressure persists, when it intensifies, and which surfaces drive it.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: Heat pressure is shaped by a coupled land-surface system rather than by isolated variables. Vegetation, moisture, built-up intensity and exposed soil interact over time and together determine relative heat intensity. The analysis converts satellite observations into decision-ready information for heat mitigation, urban resilience and asset protection.

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Where and when does heat pressure persist?
story.text: Cooling actions need to be targeted. That means detecting where and when surface shifts occur, then diagnosing the dominant drivers and prioritizing persistent hotspots.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Six indicators from monthly Sentinel-2
story.text: Monthly Sentinel-2 L2A composites with cloud masking (QA60 and SCL) and median compositing, turned into NDVI, NDWI, NDBI, BSI, emissivity and an LST proxy.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: From signal to priorities
story.text: Quality control, temporal normalization, indicator engineering, and spatial and temporal analytics. Interventions are then monitored through NDVI and emissivity gains and a lower LST proxy.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Sentinel-2 L2A
items.text: Monthly composites covering March 2023 to March 2026, from the Copernicus Sentinel-2 Level-2A archive.

items.name: Cloud and quality masking
items.text: QA60 cloud masking, plus the scene classification layer (SCL) to remove contaminated observations.

items.name: Temporal normalization
items.text: Monthly median compositing, for stable month-to-month comparability.

items.name: Indicators
items.text: NDVI, NDWI, NDBI, BSI, emissivity and LST proxy.

deliverables: Maps of the monthly indicators and of the LST proxy over the whole area of interest.
AOI-wide monthly trend analytics for the 36-month period.
Hotspot geography: persistent hotspot clusters, cooler belts and transition zones.
Risk signals and a seasonal calendar for timing preventive interventions.
An interactive map to explore the full 36-month dataset.

methods.title: Building a reliable heat-risk signal
text: Clouds and scene-to-scene variability were minimized first, so that the trends observed are more likely to reflect real surface behavior than data artifacts. The cleaned observations were then translated into six complementary indicators that track how vegetation, moisture, built-up intensity and exposed soil interact through time.

Relative heat intensity rises when vegetative cooling weakens and exposed urban surfaces dominate: higher NDBI, higher BSI, lower NDVI, lower NDWI and the emissivity signal combine into a higher LST proxy. The LST proxy is a relative heat-pressure index, not a direct temperature measurement: it supports comparison between places and months, not absolute temperature values.

steps.title: NDWI

steps.title: NDBI

steps.title: BSI

steps.title: Emissivity

gallery.caption: Figure 4. Seasonal cycle of the indices and the LST proxy over 36 months, with the heat-pressure phase (1, August 2024) and cooling phase (2, January 2025).

items.title: The seasonal cycle dominates
items.text: The LST proxy peaks in summer (August 2023 and August 2024, plus October 2025) and reaches its minimum in winter (January 2025). The area follows a repeatable seasonal surface-behavior cycle.

items.title: Index extremes coincide with LST extremes
items.text: In August 2024 the LST maximum coincides with the NDBI and BSI maxima. In January 2025 the LST minimum coincides with the NDVI maximum. More vegetation goes with less relative heat, and more built-up or dry surface with more heat.

items.title: The cycle has two phases
items.text: In the heat-pressure phase NDBI and BSI rise while NDVI and emissivity soften. In the cooling phase NDVI and emissivity recover while heat pressure declines. The NDVI minimum falls in October 2025 rather than in summer, which suggests water stress accumulated after the summer.

items.title: Hotspots are geographically stable
items.text: The same zones stay hot in March 2023 and March 2026, with low NDVI and high NDBI and BSI, while cooler belts keep higher NDVI and emissivity. Transition zones show mixed signatures with seasonal sensitivity.

items.title: Emissivity and NDWI add little
items.text: Emissivity is almost constant and does not explain the variation of the LST proxy. NDWI is low and stable, which indicates an area dominated by non-water surfaces.

limits.title: Limitations and monitoring
items: Relative index. The LST proxy is derived from the same optical indices (no thermal band), so its agreement with NDVI, NDBI and BSI is partly expected and is not independent evidence. Validation against Landsat thermal data, ECOSTRESS or weather stations is needed.
Incomplete series. January 2026 is missing from the 36-month series.
AOI averages. Area-wide averages hide neighborhood-scale variation.
Association, not causation. The data show association between surface type and relative heat, not that built-up land causes it.

subtitle: Crop Water Stress Monitoring
summary: A satellite-based prototype to monitor water use and crop water stress in Sicilian olive groves and citrus orchards, built on seasonal Sentinel-2 indices.
heroText: Seasonal Sentinel-2 composites and four spectral indices show how olive groves around Castelvetrano respond to water availability, to support irrigation planning and the control of water use.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: Agricultural water consortia struggle to trace consumption and collect fees, because they have no continuous monitoring system. This makes it hard to plan water needs and to control waste. The project proposes an integrated remote-sensing prototype, working on two target areas and designed on the model of IrriSAT and of the satellite irrigation monitoring implemented by Regione Campania. The integration of satellite data with ground sensors already in the territory, such as the SIAS agrometeorological network, is also being evaluated.

stats.label: Spectral indices: NDVI, NDWI, WDSI, SAVI
Sentinel-2 scenes in four seasonal composites

meta.Output: Seasonal index maps and terrain layers

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Water use is hard to trace and charge
story.text: Without continuous monitoring, consortia cannot tell how much water each agricultural area uses. The prototype aims to monitor consumption for each area, forecast crop water needs, spot anomalous or unauthorised withdrawals, reduce waste and support strategic planning. It targets regions, land reclamation consortia and farmers.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Sentinel-2 seasons and terrain
story.text: Seasonal Sentinel-2 composites over Castelvetrano from December 2022 to November 2023, with scenes above 25% cloud cover excluded, plus terrain layers for Sicily: elevation, slope and the Topographic Wetness Index.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: Four indices read season by season
story.text: NDVI and SAVI measure vegetation vigour, NDWI detects leaf water content and WDSI combines NDVI and NDWI to flag plants that stay green but lose water. Maps are compared across the four seasons, following an IrriSAT-style architecture.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Sentinel-2
items.text: Seasonal composites of Castelvetrano: winter (December 2022 to February 2023) from 213 scenes, spring (March to May 2023) from 209, summer (June to August 2023) from 392 and autumn (September to November 2023) from 274. Scenes with cloud cover above 25% are excluded.

items.name: Digital terrain model
items.text: Elevation (DTM) of Sicily, with slope and the Topographic Wetness Index (TWI) derived from it.

items.name: SIAS network
items.text: Local readings from the Sicilian agrometeorological network. Combining them with the satellite data (data fusion) is under evaluation, to maximise the precision of the model.

items.name: Reference model
items.text: IrriSAT, which uses Sentinel-2 to estimate crop evapotranspiration and sends registered farmers a personalised irrigation advice in millimetres of water. In Campania it is run by Ariespace with the AGEA paying agency and the SIGRIAN database.

deliverables: Seasonal NDVI, NDWI, WDSI and SAVI maps for Castelvetrano.
Terrain layers for Sicily: elevation, slope and Topographic Wetness Index.
A prototype design for irrigation monitoring on two target areas, on the model of IrriSAT.
A support framework with three functions: classification of the territory, support to the design of water needs, and monitoring at 1, 3 and 5 years.

methods.title: From satellite scenes to water stress maps
text: The prototype covers two areas. Ribera (Agrigento) has 6,000 to 7,000 ha of citrus orchards, of which 1,600 ha are DOP, on more than 1,500 farms with very fragmented land (Washington Navel, Navelina, Brasiliana and Vaniglia). Castelvetrano (Trapani) has 6,000 to 7,000 ha of olive groves (Nocellara del Belice) in the Belice valley, about 12,000 ha when neighbouring municipalities are included, on 3,000 to 4,000 farms, with 500 to 700 mm of rain per year and high land fragmentation.

The architecture is similar to IrriSAT: the satellite sees how much the plant is transpiring and the system turns it into the millimetres of water to give, avoiding waste. Water stress is read through four indices that describe different parts of the plant and soil system, and the analysis shown in this page covers Castelvetrano.

steps.title: 1. Build seasonal composites
steps.text: Sentinel-2 scenes are collected for each season, with a 25% cloud threshold, and combined into one composite per season (1,088 scenes in total).

steps.title: 2. Compute the indices
steps.text: NDVI and SAVI measure vegetation vigour, and SAVI is more reliable where soil is exposed. NDWI detects water content in the leaves. WDSI = (NDVI - NDWI) / |NDVI + NDWI| captures the plant's physiological response: it goes to zero when the two indices agree, with no stress, and rises toward +1 when vegetation is green but short of water.

steps.title: 3. Add terrain context
steps.text: Elevation, slope and the Topographic Wetness Index show where water tends to accumulate or run off, from the digital terrain model, where each pixel holds an accurate elevation.

steps.title: 4. Compare the seasons
steps.text: Maps are read season by season, to see how vegetation vigour and water content change through the year and where stress persists.

steps.title: 5. Support planning and control
steps.text: The planned service has three functions: classification of the territory and identification of the parameters that matter for agriculture, support to the design of water needs, and monitoring at 1, 3 and 5 years to verify the effects of policies and any deviations due to illicit use.

Figure 2. Data fusion concept: satellite data and readings from the SIAS weather stations are combined into one irrigation output.
Figure 3. Slope (left) and elevation (right) over Sicily, from the digital terrain model.

Figure 4. Topographic Wetness Index over Sicily. Yellow marks the highest values along valleys and coastal plains, where water accumulates. Orange marks the lowest values, on the Madonie, the Nebrodi and Etna.

main.caption: Figure 5. NDVI by season at Castelvetrano. Winter and spring show intense green and good photosynthetic activity. In summer yellow-orange dominates, reflecting water stress from heat and drought. In autumn there is a partial recovery thanks to the first rains, although inland areas remain in difficulty.

gallery.title: NDWI
gallery.caption: Figure 6. NDWI by season at Castelvetrano. Values are highest in winter and spring, when there is more humidity, reach their minimum in summer because of seasonal drought, and partly recover in autumn. In summer the leaves have lost a significant amount of water, but the tree resists. Lake Trinità appears red in winter because the formula uses NIR and SWIR, and deep water absorbs almost all NIR.

gallery.title: WDSI
gallery.caption: Figure 7. WDSI by season at Castelvetrano. The red persists through all four seasons, showing chronic water stress. The recurring blue anomaly is Lake Trinità, a permanent water body with no stress.

gallery.title: SAVI
gallery.caption: Figure 8. SAVI by season at Castelvetrano. In winter the groves show good vegetation cover, with some orange areas of bare soil between the canopies. In spring green recedes and orange advances. In summer yellow-orange dominates the whole area, and autumn stays similar with a slight recovery.

items.title: Vegetation follows a Mediterranean cycle
items.text: NDVI is highest in winter and spring, when olive trees show intense green and optimal water conditions, drops sharply in summer as the trees slow their metabolism to save water, and partly recovers in autumn.

items.title: Leaf water content peaks in the wet months
items.text: NDWI is highest in winter and spring and lowest in summer, with a partial recovery in autumn.

items.title: Water stress is chronic
items.text: NDVI and NDWI move in opposite directions: the plant keeps its chlorophyll but loses leaf water. At Castelvetrano this divergence is at its maximum and constant through the year, which explains the persistent red in the WDSI maps.

items.title: Bare soil shows between the trees
items.text: SAVI reveals exposed soil between the canopies already in winter, and low cover across the area in summer.

items.title: Terrain explains where water is retained
items.text: TWI values across Sicily are mostly medium to low (5 to 12), typical of a Mediterranean island with marked relief, steep slopes and little capacity to retain water.

subtitle: Urban Flood Risk & Predictive Maintenance of Urban Assets
summary: A web GIS platform for public administrations that combines terrain, satellite, weather and field reports to map urban flood risk and support drainage management. Developed for the Italian Space Agency (ASI).
heroText: From terrain and satellite data to flood risk maps and storm scenarios, published as GIS services and explored in a web platform with live weather and reports from the field.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: Urban flooding depends on terrain, surface sealing, rainfall and the condition of the drains. DRAINS brings these sources into one web platform built on ArcGIS. Flood risk maps and storm scenarios are computed offline from terrain and satellite data, checked, and refreshed every three to six months. Live weather forecasts and reports from citizens and field operators are layered on top, so users see both how prone an area is to flooding and what is happening now.

stats.label: Flood scenarios: blocked drains and working drains
Refresh cycle of the pre-computed risk maps
User groups: viewers, editors, administrators and citizens

meta.Data: Official flood plans, satellite, terrain model, weather forecasts, citizen and field reports
meta.Output: Flood risk maps, storm scenarios, dashboards, mobile app for maintenance crews

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Flood risk information is scattered
story.text: Official plans, terrain, satellite images, weather forecasts and reports from the territory come in different formats and update cycles. Public administrations need them in one place to see where water accumulates and which drains need attention.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Official, satellite and field data
story.text: Regional and national flood plans (PAI and PGRA) and municipal data, satellite imagery and a digital terrain model, weather forecasts from external services, and geolocated reports and drain surveys collected on the ground.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: Compute offline, publish, overlay live data
story.text: Risk maps and scenarios are produced with GIS analysis, validated and published as standard map services on ArcGIS Enterprise. A web application and a mobile app for maintenance crews consume them, with weather and reports added as live layers.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Official flood and land data
items.text: Hydrogeological and flood-risk plans (PAI, PGRA) and municipal datasets, harmonised in a single geospatial model.

items.name: Satellite and terrain
items.text: Satellite data such as Sentinel-2 and a digital terrain model, used to derive the Topographic Wetness Index (TWI) and other terrain factors.

items.name: Land cover and context
items.text: Land use and cover, sealed surfaces, green areas, buildings, roads and administrative boundaries.

items.name: Weather forecasts
items.text: Forecasts and environmental data from external APIs, updated in near real time and shown as context next to the risk maps.

items.name: Reports and field surveys
items.text: Reports from citizens and field operators, plus drain surveys, collected with Survey123 and Field Maps.

deliverables: A flood risk map showing how prone each area is to water accumulation, based on terrain indicators such as the TWI.
Two storm scenarios: one with blocked drains, with more intense flooding, and one with working drains, where some areas still flood.
Live layers for weather forecasts, citizen reports and the state of the drainage network.
Dashboards with report counts, status and distribution, filters by area, time and event type, and map export to PDF and images.
A mobile app for maintenance crews to see, update and add reports and drains in the field.

methods.title: From heterogeneous data to decision maps
text: All sources are validated, checked for quality and reprojected to metric reference systems, so that distances and areas are measured correctly. They are then aligned on a regular 25 m modelling grid, so the model does not claim more precision than the observations support.

Risk maps and scenarios are generated offline with GIS analysis and published as map services after validation. Live weather and reports do not change the models: they add the current picture on top of the pre-computed maps. Drains are handled as a scenario modifier, so that better drainage never raises the estimated risk.

In plain words: the TWI (Topographic Wetness Index) shows where water tends to gather; PAI and PGRA are the official plans on hydrogeological and flood risk; a storm scenario is a simulation of heavy rain; storm drains are the street inlets that carry water away.

steps.title: 1. Collect
steps.text: Static data (official plans, satellite, terrain) is imported periodically. Weather and reports arrive continuously.

steps.title: 2. Validate and harmonise

steps.title: 3. Compute risk
steps.text: Terrain indicators such as the TWI describe how prone each area is to water accumulation.

steps.title: 4. Model scenarios
steps.text: Flood modelling compares storm events with blocked and with working drains.

steps.title: 5. Publish
steps.text: Validated maps become interoperable services (REST, WMS, WFS) every three to six months.

steps.title: 6. Consult and update
steps.text: Users explore maps and dashboards; citizens and crews send reports that feed the same picture.

summary: A field trial of Starlink satellite backhaul to bring ultra-broadband connectivity to remote Lombardy villages.
heroText: Traffic from virtual villages served by fibre, copper and wireless is collected at regional access points and carried over Starlink to Milan, to test whether satellite links can support ultra-broadband services.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: The experimentation tests satellite connectivity as backhaul for ultra-broadband access in Lombardy. Traffic from the Virtual Villages, reached through FTTH, FTTC and FWA access networks, is collected at an Access Network Collection Point (PRRA) and forwarded over an L2VPN on MPLS carried by the Starlink infrastructure to the aggregation point in Milan Caldera, then routed to the Internet. Quality is measured under load at each PRRA.

stats.label: Starlink antennas per PRRA, at most

meta.Data: Network throughput, latency and packet loss

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Ultra-broadband beyond the terrestrial network
story.text: Remote villages are hard to serve with terrestrial backhaul. The trial checks whether Starlink links can carry the traffic of fibre, copper and wireless access networks with enough quality for everyday services.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Throughput, latency and packet loss
story.text: Download and upload speed per Virtual Village, UDP latency (a ping under load), TCP round trip time and packet loss, measured under simulated load at the PRRAs.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: Starlink as MPLS backhaul
story.text: Each PRRA aggregates its villages and sends their traffic over an L2VPN on MPLS carried by Starlink. Capacity grows with the number of antennas, up to about 2 Gbps in download and 240 Mbps in upload with six antennas.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Virtual Villages
items.text: Villages reached through FTTH on optical fibre, FTTC on copper and FWA on wireless access networks.

items.name: PRRA equipment
items.text: Each PRRA has 6 Starlink Enterprise kits with modem, 1 KVH satellite kit with a 74 cm antenna, 1 Davis weather station, 1 Cisco NCS 540 aggregation router and 1 Huawei EA5801E-FL16 OLT.

items.name: Weather data
items.text: Weather stations at each PRRA, to correlate network quality with weather conditions in the next phase.

deliverables: Speed per Virtual Village, in download and upload.
UDP latency, TCP round trip time and packet loss.
A scalable design for satellite backhaul with MPLS multiplexing.

methods.title: From the access network to the Internet
text: Villages are reached by three access technologies: FTTH on optical fibre, FTTC on copper and FWA on wireless. Their traffic reaches the PRRA over terrestrial links, then crosses Starlink on an L2VPN over MPLS to the Milan Caldera aggregation point and on to Internet.

Scalability comes from aggregating several Starlink antennas, from MPLS multiplexing and from the integration with operators' Layer 2 networks, which allows the available bandwidth to be shared dynamically between terminals.

steps.title: 2. Carry it over Starlink

steps.title: 3. Load the network
steps.text: Traffic from the simulated users of each Virtual Village is generated in download and upload.

steps.title: 4. Measure
steps.text: Speed, UDP latency, TCP round trip time and packet loss are recorded at each PRRA.

summary: A European project to build certified, Galileo-based timing receivers that give critical infrastructure secure and resilient time synchronization.
heroText: CLEPSYDRA, funded by the EUSPA Fundamental Elements programme, develops a cost-efficient timing receiver platform at TRL 7/8 based on Galileo Second Generation.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: CLEPSYDRA aims to design, develop and bring to market a new generation of certified Galileo-based timing receivers, ensuring secure, resilient and high-precision time synchronization for critical infrastructure. Building on the Timing Service Message (TSM) and Open Service Navigation Message Authentication (OS-NMA) of Galileo Second Generation (G2G), it enables a European-level standardized timing service compliant with CEN/CENELEC EN 16605:2024. Its mission is to strengthen Europe's technological autonomy in time and synchronization services, with a high-performance and cost-efficient receiver platform that protects energy, telecommunications, finance and transport networks against cyber and geopolitical threats. BIP supports the exploitation and commercialization of the product, with strategy and go-to-market, business analysis, economic-financial models, stakeholder engagement, communication and dissemination.

stats.label: Core sectors: energy, telecom, finance, transport
ASPIS accuracy in the Jammertest 2025 time-offset test

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Trusted time for critical infrastructure
story.text: Recent GNSS jamming, spoofing and signal-loss events show that a disruption can mean cancelled flights, ship navigation problems and major economic losses. A UK Government report counted over 1,000 GNSS interference events in one year at a London Stock Exchange detector, and estimated losses of £7.64 million for a seven-day outage.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Galileo G2G, threats and sector needs
story.text: Galileo Second Generation timing services (TSM and OS-NMA), the main spoofing and meaconing attack scenarios, and the synchronization needs, service levels and regulations of energy, telecom, finance, transport and other critical sectors.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: A certified, standardized timing platform
story.text: A multi-constellation, multi-frequency receiver with a time and frequency core, anti-jamming and ML-based anti-spoofing, built on EN 16605:2024 and designed to address the emerging IEEE P1952 standard for resilient PNT user equipment.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Galileo G2G
items.text: Timing Service Message disseminated on the I/NAV message, with monitoring of GST and UTC accuracy, and OS-NMA authentication.

items.name: Standards
items.text: CEN/CENELEC EN 16605:2024 for Galileo timing receivers, and the emerging IEEE P1952 for resilient PNT user equipment.

items.name: Consortium
items.text: Thales Alenia Space Italia (GNSS receivers), ELPROMA Elektronika (resilient time synchronization, Poland), PikTime Systems (time transfer and time-frequency software, Poland), GEA Space (navigation and anti-spoofing, Czech Republic) and BIP (exploitation and go-to-market).

items.name: Service levels
items.text: Galileo Timing Service Levels: maximum time error of 1000 ns for SL1, 100 ns for SL2, and 15 ns (GST) and 30 ns (UTC) for SL3.

deliverables: A cost-efficient, high-performance timing receiver platform at TRL 7/8.
A certified Galileo-based receiver for critical infrastructure.
A central point of trusted UTC time, with Galileo as the single source and GPS as a backup.
Support to a European-standardized timing service.

methods.title: From Galileo signals to trusted time
text: CLEPSYDRA is not an ordinary GNSS time server. It is meant to act as an enterprise (IT) and industrial (OT) time firewall, a central point of trusted UTC time that can optionally be isolated from the physical satellites through RF filtering and GNSS simulation.

The receiver tracks Galileo E1, E5a/E5b and E6, processes the Timing Service Message, applies OS-NMA authentication and T-RAIM integrity monitoring, and falls back to holdover when GNSS is lost. It outputs 1 PPS and 10 MHz, and distributes time over PTP, NTP and IRIG.

steps.title: 1. Define sector needs
steps.text: Collect timing requirements and Galileo service levels for energy, telecom, finance, transport and other sectors.

steps.title: 2. Receive and process Galileo
steps.text: Multi-constellation, dual-frequency tracking, TSM decoding, OS-NMA and T-RAIM, with removal of satellites that fail the local barriers.

steps.title: 3. Detect and mitigate attacks
steps.text: RF interference detection and mitigation, plus ASPIS, a machine-learning spoofing detector patented by GEA Space.

steps.title: 4. Keep and distribute time
steps.text: A GNSS-disciplined time and frequency core with holdover, delivering 1 PPS, 10 MHz, PTP, NTP and IRIG.

steps.title: 5. Certify and align with standards
steps.text: Align the receiver with EN 16605:2024 and with the five levels of IEEE P1952: detect and alert, recover, resist, withstand and verify.

items.title: Finance
items.text: A UK Government report (October 2023) found over 1,000 GNSS interference events in one year at a London Stock Exchange detector, and estimated £7.64 million of losses for a seven-day GNSS outage.

items.title: Telecommunications
items.text: Poland's National Institute of Telecommunications (January 2026) warns that GNSS disruptions can destabilise mobile networks, specialised communication systems and emergency services.

items.title: Aviation
items.text: Repeated GNSS disruptions forced Finnair to suspend flights to Tartu for one month in 2024. Reuters reported two flights returning because GPS interference prevented landing.

items.title: Maritime
items.text: Finnish and Estonian authorities (June 2025) warned that GNSS disruption in the Gulf of Finland was causing positioning problems, autopilot failures and a higher accident risk.

items.title: Desynchronization as a cyber threat
items.text: The consortium points out that desynchronizing IT and OT systems is a cheap and non-invasive way to cause denial of service at critical infrastructure, and one that the growing Industry 4.0 market may not perceive.

items.title: Energy (SL2)
items.text: Power transmission networks use Wide Area Monitoring, Protection and Control systems and phasor measurement units. If a unit or the central server drifts out of sync, valid data can be rejected and wrong protection actions triggered. Relevant regulation: NIS2 / CER and the EU System Operation Guideline.

items.title: Telecom (SL2/SL3)
items.text: 5G radio access and core networks need precise phase and frequency, kept through GNSS outages by holdover. CLEPSYDRA adds anti-jamming, anti-spoofing, OS-NMA and T-RAIM. Relevant standards: ITU-T G.8271/G.8272, 3GPP and NIS2.

items.title: Finance (SL1)
items.text: Trading venues, high-frequency trading and banking data centers need UTC-traceable timestamps and an audit trail. Relevant regulation: MiFID II / MiFIR RTS 25, NIS2 / CER, and eIDAS and ETSI trust-service standards.

items.title: Transport and others (SL1)
items.text: Air traffic control, rail and waterworks depend on synchronized nodes for event sequencing, monitoring and safe operations. Relevant regulation: NIS2 / CER and ERTMS.

subtitle: Rail Demand Forecasting for Major International Events
summary: A methodology to estimate how much extra high-speed rail demand a major event generates in Italy, using historical rail data, mobile network data and past events.
heroText: From past events and historical rail and mobility data to the extra high-speed rail passengers expected for a major international event in 2027.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: The product estimates the extra rail demand that a major international event adds to the high-speed connections towards a large Italian metropolitan area. It builds on historical rail data, mobile network data, air passenger data and a benchmark of past events and supports the planning of rail services for the event.

stats.label: Main data sources: rail, mobile network, air

meta.Area: Major Italian metropolitan area, high-speed network
meta.Data: Historical rail data, mobile network data, IATA, event benchmark
meta.Output: Extra rail demand by origin and corridor

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Historical series describe normal days, not event days
story.text: Rail demand can change during a major event, and historical series alone do not show by how much. Planners need to know how many extra passengers to expect, separately from ordinary mobility and where they come from.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Rail, mobile network, air and event data
story.text: Historical rail demand from a leading European high-speed rail operator, aggregated mobile network data, IATA air passenger data, a benchmark of comparable national and international events and the forecasting models already in use.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: From expected visitors to high-speed rail flows
story.text: Starting from the expected number of visitors, the model estimates the share that travels by high-speed rail and splits it by geographic origin along the main corridors. Historical demand gives the ordinary baseline, to which the event lift is added.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Historical rail demand
items.text: Passenger flows and origin–destination relations on the main high-speed corridors, from a leading European high-speed rail operator.

items.name: Mobile network data
items.text: Aggregated trips between geographic areas, used to describe overall mobility flows and their spatial distribution.

items.name: IATA air passenger data
items.text: Air passenger flows and origin–destination relations, to compare air with the other transport modes.

items.name: Major event benchmark
items.text: Location, dates, type and attendance of national and international events.

deliverables: An assessment of the current forecasting processes and models, with the departments involved, the data they use and the main improvement needs.
A benchmark of traditional and innovative forecasting methods, with a review of the available data sources and what each can be used for.
A methodology to estimate the extra rail demand of a major international event, based on comparable past events and the combined mobility data.

methods.title: From raw data to the final product
text: The work starts with a review of the current forecasting processes and models, and of the departments involved in planning the rail offer. Forecasting methods and mobility data sources are then compared to choose the ones that can be added to the current process. Comparable major events are mapped, historical rail and mobility data are collected and analyzed, and the results are used to build the lift model for the extra demand of a major international event.

The model is top-down: it starts from the expected visitors and works down to the high-speed rail share and its origin. Rail, mobile network and air passenger data are used together to maximize the model accuracy.

items.text: Current models can be improved mainly by taking external factors, such as major events, into account.

items.title: Data work better together
items.text: Each dataset covers only part of the picture. Rail, mobile network and air data are more useful together than alone.

items.title: Origin of extra flows
items.text: The top-down approach separates the high-speed rail share of event demand and shows where the extra passengers come from.

items: Historical data are not always consistent or detailed enough to rebuild mobility flows and event demand precisely.
The model is applied to a one-of-a-kind event, so comparisons with past events necessarily rely on assumptions.

subtitle: Building a Regional Smart Ticketing Ecosystem
summary: A regional Account-Based Ticketing ecosystem that combines operator sales channels, validation data and integrated fare rules to give passengers a seamless mobility experience across Calabria Region.
heroText: From passenger access and validation to fare calculation and operator settlement, a shared ABT architecture connects every step of the journey within one interoperable regional ecosystem.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: The project turns fare catalogues, sales data, validation data and operators' technology assets into a regional Account-Based Ticketing ecosystem for public transport services across Calabria. It is built around a shared architecture for ticketing, payment, validation and settlement across urban, extra-urban and rail services.

meta.Data: Fare products, sales, validation and technology-asset data

story.label: The challenge
story.title: From fragmented ticketing to one interoperable regional ecosystem
story.text: Regional ticketing systems remain fragmented across products, sales channels, validation processes and technologies. Limited interoperability hinders seamless travel, integrated payments and consistent passenger experience.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Transport, Commercial and Operator Technology AS-IS assessment
story.text: The assessment analyses transport demand, revenues, ticketing, fleet, onboard equipment, sales channels, validation methods, system architectures and payment models. A key focus is functional requirements design and technical coordination and oversight of development activities, based on project documents, questionnaires and working sessions.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: Connecting the dots across the ticketing ecosystem
story.text: The approach aligns passenger experience, operating models and technology architecture through ticketing benchmarks, supplier assessment, stakeholder and interface mapping. These inform pilot design, target ABT architecture, governance, integrated-fare principles and a phased rollout roadmap.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Transport operator landscape
items.text: Operator services, fleet characteristics, onboard equipment, ticket products, sales channels and existing technologies, collected through project documentation and operator engagement.

items.name: Transport simulation data
items.text: Transport demand, passenger flows and service volumes derived from transport simulation model outputs.

items.name: Financial and Fare Data
items.text: Fare structures, ticket prices, passenger revenues, ticket sales and payment models, obtainable from transport operators and regional transport authorities.

deliverables: Target architecture, functional requirements and governance model for the regional Account-Based Ticketing ecosystem, supporting the implementation and management of prepaid and postpaid ticketing services.
Integrated fare model that enables seamless travel across rail, urban and extra-urban services through a common fare framework.
Pilot and regional rollout roadmap outlining implementation priorities, technical coordination activities and the progressive extension to additional operators and services.

methods.title: From raw data to the final product
text: Fare catalogues, sales data, validation data and operators’ technology inventories are collected and analysed across Calabria’s public transport ecosystem. The information is used to assess technological maturity, compare alternative implementation scenarios and define the scope of a pilot deployment. Operational and validation data generated during the pilot are then examined to identify critical issues, validate key assumptions and consolidate lessons learned. The resulting evidence is used to define governance arrangements, technical requirements and the target architecture for the regional Account-Based Ticketing ecosystem.

The pilot-first approach is chosen to validate operational, technological and fare-integration assumptions before regional deployment. The assessment focuses on operators’ existing ticketing systems, validation technologies and fare structures to ensure that governance, architecture and implementation choices reflect the characteristics of Calabria’s transport ecosystem.

items: The pilot covers a limited set of operators, services and travel scenarios. Additional operational evidence is required to validate the applicability of the proposed model at regional scale.

subtitle: Spatial Analysis For Passenger Information
summary: A spatial analysis combines public transport network data, regional mapping and mobility services to identify priority hubs for passenger information kiosks in Lombardy, alongside a regional data platform feasibility study.
heroText: From stop-level services and routes within 450 m to a Connectivity Indicator, the analysis identifies 30 priority hubs to guide the placement of passenger information kiosks.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: The project identifies priority locations for passenger information kiosks in Lombardy by combining transport network data, mapping and information on mobility services. Spatial analysis supports the selection of 30 hubs, while a feasibility study compares three options for a regional platform managing static and real-time data under Action 2.8.2 of the 2021–2027 Regional PR FESR Programme.

stats.label: Service trips across timetable validity periods

meta.Area: Lombardy, Italy; detailed analysis in municipalities with an approved Sustainable Urban Mobility Plan
meta.Data: Muoversi in Lombardia, Regione Lombardia Geoportal, ISTAT, Ecomobs
meta.Output: Hub database, indicator and priority selection

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Locating information kiosks at useful interchange points
story.text: Services and operators form a regional network with uneven interchange opportunities. The challenge is to identify hubs where information kiosks can help passengers access services and make connections, while assessing how a regional platform can integrate travel information.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Stops, routes and mobility services across Lombardy
story.text: The analysis links stops, routes, itineraries and operators with infrastructure, shared and electric mobility services. In municipalities with an approved Sustainable Urban Mobility Plan, mobility points and routes are assessed within 450 m of stops. Regional data assets and platform options are also reviewed.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: Comparing nearby services with a Connectivity Indicator
story.text: Tableau links stop, route and operator records, while QGIS supports spatial analysis. Mobility points and routes within 450 m receive equal importance in a Connectivity Indicator. Hub comparisons and available shared mobility information support the selection of 30 priority locations.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Mobility network and services
items.text: Muoversi in Lombardia provides stops, routes, itineraries, operators and published service trips across the respective timetable validity periods.

items.name: Regional mapping
items.text: The Regione Lombardia Geoportal provides administrative boundaries and mobility infrastructure, including railways, stations, metro lines, roads and cycle networks.

items.name: Population and employment
items.text: ISTAT provides population data and the regional Geoportal provides employment data to characterise the study area.

items.name: Mobility planning and services
items.text: Municipal mobility plans identify planning status, while Ecomobs and available service information support the assessment of the mobility context.

deliverables: A geospatial database and network maps describe mobility services and routes around public transport stops.
A Connectivity Indicator and a selection of 30 priority hubs support the placement of passenger information kiosks.
A feasibility study compares three options for a regional platform managing static and real-time mobility data.

methods.title: From raw data to the final product
text: Stop, route, itinerary and operator records are linked through joins in Tableau and organised with geographic data in QGIS. Municipalities with an approved Sustainable Urban Mobility Plan define the detailed study area. A circular buffer of 450 m is generated around each selected stop. Mobility points are counted by category, together with routes intersecting each buffer. A Connectivity Indicator gives equal importance to total mobility points and route counts. Comparisons, supplemented by available shared mobility information, identify 30 priority hubs for passenger information kiosks.

The buffer provides a consistent geometric catchment for comparing stops. The indicator combines the presence of mobility points and routes; it does not measure timetable frequency or passenger flows. The source database covers all transport modes, including stops outside Lombardy and services beyond local public transport.

subtitle: Public Transit Digital Observatory
summary: Interactive dashboards mapping urban and suburban bus and rail services across Calabria and integrating passenger data to support the Region in evidence-based public transport planning and service optimization.
heroText: The system provides a picture of where public transport services operate, where routes overlap, and how they are used. It enables the Region to redesign local public transport based on evidence.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text:
Calabria Region has started a data-driven review of its local public transport (TPL) services. The aim is to use the information already available to understand whether supply matches the needs of demand, to assess the efficiency and quality of the service, and to make the best use of the resources allocated to TPL. This calls for several sources to be read together: service usage, operation and performance, and territorial and mobility data.
After developing the regional multimodal transport model, the team held a large body of supply and demand data. This project turns it into an interactive tool made of several dashboards, which maps urban and extra-urban bus and rail services across the region, links them to surveyed and simulated passengers, and helps public administration staff spot weak points and opportunities for rescheduling.

meta.Area: Calabria, Italy: urban and extra-urban bus and regional rail.

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Reviewing services with information scattered across sources
story.text: The Region aims to redesign public transport services based on objective evidence, using indicators to assess how effectively supply meets demand and to evaluate operational efficiency and service quality. However, the required data are fragmented across multiple sources and formats, covering service usage (passenger volumes and ticketing data), operational performance (trips, vehicle-kilometers, municipalities and provinces served, and route overlaps), and territorial characteristics and demand patterns (school mobility and socio-economic data)

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Integrated analysis of service supply, operational programmes and passenger demand
story.text: GTFS timetables and model-derived shapefiles of bus and rail routes and stops were integrated with scheduled service programmes to compare GTFS-based supply against planned operations. The comparison was embedded in the dashboards to assess GTFS data consistency and visualize the geographical distribution and concentration of discrepancies across Calabria. Passenger demand was analyzed using survey data from bus routes, boarding and alighting figures at railway stations, and passenger volumes and passenger-kilometers estimated by the regional transport model.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: An integrated view of coverage, service overlaps and performance
story.text: The dashboards address three key planning questions: where public transport services operate and how well they connect the territory; where routes overlap and opportunities exist for better coordination; and how line-level performance compares with the supply offered, highlighting potential areas for service improvement.

items.name: Passenger surveys
items.text: Passengers boarded and alighted on bus lines and at rail stops. For each line the value covers the whole itinerary and is the average of boardings and alightings.

items.name: GIS processing
items.text: Shapefiles enriched with values used in the maps, such as the distance between each bus stop and the nearest rail station, which allows analysis within a variable radius around stations.

items.name: Simulated demand
items.text: Passengers and passenger-km per line from the regional transport model, shown next to surveyed passengers in the line performance dashboard and compared with them through the GEH statistic.

deliverables: Use Case 1, supply summary: a regional map of extra-urban and urban bus and rail stops, with operators by colour and ridership by line thickness, plus tables of operators and lines and five ready analyses by province, municipality, consortium, operator and line.

Use Case 2, origin-destination relations served by bus and rail: services by origin or destination municipality or station with a radius for nearby bus stops, trips by arrival hour, and timetables with stops and travel times, with six ready analyses.
Use case 3, line performance: supply in the programme and in the model, surveyed and simulated demand with GEH, occupancy indicators and the hourly profile of trips.

methods.title: From raw data to the final product
text: The dashboard is the front end of a data workflow: each step aligns a new source to the same lines, stops and places, so that officials can move from a regional overview down to a single line or relation: 1-Prepare the supply data: the GTFS data loaded into the regional transport model are exported as shapefiles of bus and rail lines and stops. Programmed supply, derived from the operators’ service schedules, is used as a reference to assess the consistency of the GTFS data imported into the model, which may differ slightly from the planned service; 2 - Enrich with GIS: GIS processing adds values useful for representation, such as the distance of every bus stop from the nearest rail station, so users can look at all services around a station within a radius they choose; 3- Attach demand and indicators: surveyed passengers, boardings and alightings are linked to lines and rail stops, and passengers and passenger-km simulated by the model are added. Indicators include seats offered, occupancy, passenger-km per seat-km and GEH.

subtitle: Regional Integrated Digital Ticketing Platform
summary: CSR Digitale is Lombardy’s integrated digital ticketing platform, connecting operator systems, transport service data and fares to manage digital tickets and passes and support journey reconstruction and best-fare calculation.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: CSR Digitale is Lombardy’s integrated digital ticketing platform for pre-paid tickets and post-paid bank-card journeys. It connects operator systems, service data and fare rules to support ticket management, journey reconstruction, best-fare calculation and revenue-allocation reporting. APIs, a mobile SDK and a Travel Planner provide supporting tools.

meta.Data: TPLombardia, operator ticketing and validation systems, fare catalogues, fare-zone mapping, payment outcomes
meta.Output: Digital ticketing platform and supporting tools

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Making digital tickets interoperable across operators
story.text: Separate operator systems fragment digital ticket management and limit fare integration across services. The challenge is to create a common regional platform that connects tickets, validations and journeys, supporting integrated fares and revenue allocation based on actual network use.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Ticket lifecycles, transport services and fare rules
story.text: The analysis covers pre-paid and post-paid ticket lifecycles, operator interactions, validation events and payment outcomes. Stops, routes, timetables and geometries are combined with fare catalogues and zones to define the information needed for journey reconstruction and fare calculation.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: A shared platform with common integration services
story.text: CSR Digitale brings ticket management, journey reconstruction and fare calculation into a common regional system. Application programming interfaces (APIs) connect operators, the mobile SDK supports secure digital ticket presentation, and the Travel Planner supports route simulation and fare checks.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Transport service data
items.text: TPLombardia and operators provide stops, routes, trips, timetables and geometries through standard exchange formats, including General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) and NeTEx.

items.name: Fare catalogues and zones

A suite of 45 integration APIs and a mobile SDK support operator system connections, ticket activation, signed barcode generation and cryptographic key management.
A regional Travel Planner supports operators and CSR Digitale with multimodal itinerary simulation, fare checks and journey reconstruction.

methods.title: From raw data to the final product
text: Service data, fare catalogues, zones and operator records establish the platform’s reference data. Operator systems exchange ticket issuance, activation and validation information with CSR Digitale through APIs. For post-paid journeys, payment aliases link validation events across operators. The platform uses service and validation data to reconstruct journeys and apply fare rules, including best-fare logic, while recording payment outcomes. Reconstructed travel supports revenue-allocation reporting. The mobile SDK supports secure ticket presentation; the Travel Planner assists route simulation and fare checks.

Account-based ticketing links digital ticket information to regional account references. Stable stop, line and trip identifiers and complete route geometries support journey reconstruction. The SDK provides shared app security functions; the Travel Planner supports operational simulations.

subtitle: From Data To Traffic Simulation
summary: The project combines monitoring data, road network information and travel demand to update the metropolitan Doha traffic model, supporting flow forecasts, scenario assessments and detailed junction analysis.
heroText: From quality-checked traffic counts to calibrated demand and junction simulations, the model supports network assessments and traffic management during exceptional events.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: The project updates the transport model for metropolitan Doha, Qatar, using traffic monitoring observations, road network characteristics and travel demand. Network simulation and detailed junction models support traffic flow analysis, forecasting and assessment of interventions, including during exceptional events.

stats.label: Detector entries in the inventory tables

meta.Data: Detector inventories, traffic counts and speeds, day-type calendar, road network, O/D demand, real-time monitoring feeds
meta.Output: Calibrated network and junction simulation models

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Integrating monitoring observations into a usable traffic model
story.text: Multiple monitoring technologies produce overlapping records, gaps and inconsistent traffic counts. The challenge is to update the network and travel demand model so that it supports strategic analysis, flow forecasting and operational assessments during exceptional events.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Road network, travel demand and monitoring data
story.text: The analysis covers road network attributes, Origin–Destination (O/D) demand matrices, traffic counts and speeds. Checks assess availability, temporal coverage and consistency across six day types. Selected junctions are examined in detail to identify vehicle interactions and local bottlenecks.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: Connecting network calibration and junction simulation
story.text: The approach combines data reliability checks, macroscopic model calibration and junction microsimulation. PTV Visum and PTV Optima support network modelling and monitoring integration; PTV Vissim provides detailed assessments of vehicle movements at ten selected junctions.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Detector inventories
items.text: Two database inventory tables list 10,198 and 697 detector entries, with identifiers and associations to count locations and the model.

items.name: Traffic observations and feeds
items.text: Historical count tables and real-time monitoring feeds provide vehicle counts, speeds and vehicle classifications where available; overlapping sources are not independent observations.

items.name: Day-type calendar
items.text: The calendar distinguishes Ramadan weekdays and Fridays/Saturdays, non-Ramadan school and non-school weekdays, and non-Ramadan Fridays and Saturdays.

items.name: Model network and O/D demand
items.text: The existing model provides link and node geometries, capacity, free-flow speed, lane counts and Origin–Destination demand matrices.

deliverables: An updated and calibrated macroscopic model represents the mobility network and supports analysis of changing traffic flows.
Statically and dynamically calibrated O/D matrices align travel demand with the traffic counts used for calibration.
Ten PTV Vissim microsimulation models support detailed junction assessments and comparison of potential traffic improvements.

methods.title: From raw data to the final product
text: Detector inventories are matched to count locations and model links. Traffic counts and speeds are aggregated by detector, date and hour, checked for completeness and consistency, and grouped into six day types. Reliable counts support updates to the network and static O/D calibration with T-Flow Fuzzy. Dynamic Origin–Destination Matrix Estimation (DODME) then adjusts demand using vehicle propagation times and the dynamic assignment matrix from the PTV Visum DAM add-in. Observed and simulated flows are compared using GEH; ten PTV Vissim models support detailed junction analysis.

Reliability checks operate first at detector level and then at count location level. They assess completeness, flow-to-capacity ratios, changes between consecutive hours and daytime versus nighttime flows. Sensitivity analysis adjusts selection thresholds to the dataset; overlapping sources are assessed without summing them as independent observations.

items.text: Demand and model parameters are calibrated across six day types. Agreement is assessed through the share of links with GEH at or below 5.

items.title: Junction analysis models
items.text: Ten PTV Vissim models represent vehicle interactions and local bottlenecks, providing a basis for comparing potential traffic improvements.

limits.title: Limitations and next steps
items: Data selection depends on reliability thresholds adjusted through sensitivity analysis. Real-time representation depends on the availability, quality and continuity of monitoring feeds.

Microsimulation covers selected junctions and requires updates when geometry, traffic control or demand changes. The source gives no percentage of links meeting GEH ≤ 5, so the threshold alone does not quantify calibration performance.
next: Regular updates to the network, O/D demand and source datasets to reflect changes in metropolitan mobility.
Extension of microsimulation to other priority junctions, comparison of proposed interventions.

subtitle: Shared Mobility For Underserved Rural Communities
summary: Omnibus uses spatial, transport and stakeholder data to design shared, demand-responsive journeys linking rural communities in Reggio Calabria to essential services and public transport.
heroText: From local mobility needs and transport mapping to digitally managed bookings and shared journeys, Omnibus connects dispersed rural origins to essential destinations and transport hubs.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: Omnibus provides a digitally managed demand-responsive transport (DRT) service in the Metropolitan City of Reggio Calabria, with an initial pilot in the Area Grecanica. Demographic data, transport mapping and stakeholder input inform connections to essential services and existing public transport. The model offers a basis for adaptation to similar low-demand areas.

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Connecting dispersed communities to essential destinations
story.text: Low-demand areas in Reggio Calabria combine dispersed settlements with limited public transport. Scheduled services struggle to meet demand that varies across places and times, limiting access to essential destinations for residents with fewer travel alternatives.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Local mobility needs, transport provision and target users
story.text: The analysis combines ISTAT 2022 demographics, mapped transport services and operators, low-demand areas, local points of interest and planning documents. Stakeholder questionnaires and user personas describe mobility needs, including those of older people and people with disabilities.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: A coordinated service model supported by digital platforms
story.text: A many-to-few service connects dispersed origins to key destinations and existing public transport. Three applications support passengers, drivers and the control centre, while the operating model, business plan and communication strategy define how the service works.

items.name: ISTAT 2022

methods.title: From raw data to the final product
text: The workflow starts with demographic data, transport mapping and a review of local planning and regulatory documents. Stakeholder consultations, questionnaires and user personas identify travel needs and key destinations. These inputs inform the many-to-few service model, governance arrangements, business plan and communication strategy. Passenger, driver and control centre applications then support bookings, payments, real-time communication and route optimisation. Pilot monitoring records service use, booking channels and journey patterns to inform service adjustments.

The many-to-few model connects dispersed origins to a limited set of essential destinations and transport hubs. A responsive web app and a dedicated call centre provide complementary booking channels. Advance and real-time bookings support flexibility, while assisted booking helps retain access for users who do not rely on digital tools.

subtitle: A Multimodal Transport Model for Calabria
summary: How a multimodal simulation model of Calabria was rebuilt from mobile-phone, vehicle and public transport data, and what it gives the Region for planning local public transport.
heroText: A regional multimodal transport model reproduces how people move across Calabria. It gives the Region an objective base to tune services and compare policy and service options before choosing.

overview.title: Project at a glance
overview.text: In response to changing mobility needs in Calabria, driven by demographic shifts and evolving travel patterns, the project develops a multimodal transport model that combines big data with traffic counts, boarding data and census statistics, while capturing both school-term and summer travel patterns. This enables the Region to assess transport service needs, compare different scenarios and make evidence-based planning decisions.

stats.label: Approx. kilometers of road network modelled

meta.Area: Calabria, Italy, with neighbouring regions, the rest of Italy and the Strait of Messina
meta.Data: Mobile-phone and floating-car matrices, traffic counts, GTFS timetables, boarding data, census data
meta.Output: Multimodal demand matrices by scenario, time band and mode, and a calibrated model of road and public transport networks

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Planning local public transport on an outdated picture
story.text: The Region needs to adapt services to a population that is shrinking and ageing, and to demand that changes by season, day and hour. But the last regional matrices date, traditional surveys are costly and quickly outdated, and public transport boarding data are aggregated and incomplete. There is no single, consistent view of how people travel and of how supply, fares and infrastructure shape their choices.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Big data checked against observed counts
story.text: Hourly origin-destination matrices from mobile-phone and floating-car data for two periods, traffic counts, boarding and alighting data on bus, rail and ferry services, commuting and census data, school locations and GTFS timetables. Each source fills a gap in the others and is used either to build or to check the model.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: Rebuild, split, assign, check
story.text: The classic four-stage model is adapted: generation and distribution come directly from the corrected phone matrix, with school trips estimated separately. Demand is then split between car, public transport and Park & Ride, assigned to the road and public transport networks, and calibrated against observed data.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Big Data
items.text: Mobile-phone matrices: hourly origin-destination trips from mobile-network data; Floating-car data: sampled trips from vehicle black boxes, for private and commercial vehicle.

items.name: Observed data

items.name: Transport supply
items.text: Commercial road graph, regional rail graph, GTFS timetables for bus and rail services, ferry services for the Strait of Messina crossings, and fare systems from the regional programme.

items.name: Territorial data
items.text: Population on census cells, commuting matrices, upper-secondary school locations and enrolment.

deliverables: Demand matrices for six scenarios (school term and summer, weekday, Saturday and Sunday), by time band (6 in winter, 5 in summer, plus daily totals) and by mode: car, public transport and Park & Ride.
A calibrated modal split model, integrating road and public transport networks, fares, Park & Ride zones, ready to load and evaluate any demand scenario
Insights into seasonal and hourly service variations, travel demand between zones, school-related mobility by zone, and road and service network loading to identify congestion and spare capacity

story.label: The challenge
story.title: Fragmented visibility over a city-scale service
story.text: Waste collection and street cleaning in Rome involve fleets, facilities and field teams spread over a large area. Reports, vehicle positions and asset data were handled in separate tools, so coordinating interventions and measuring service levels in time was hard.

story.label: What was analyzed
story.title: Fleet, sensor, report and planning data
story.text: GPS positions of the collection fleet, IoT sensor data from bins, roll-off containers and other assets, geo-referenced citizen reports, service planning data and satellite imagery. All are mapped on a GIS model of Rome and refreshed in near real time.

story.label: Our approach
story.title: A digital twin backed by a new operating model
story.text: We start from a technology assessment and a benchmark of comparable operations centres. We then design the to-be technology and process model, define KPIs and dashboards, and set the procedures the control room uses to manage reports and interventions.

data.title: Data sources

items.name: Fleet GPS
items.text: GPS positions of AMA collection vehicles, used to follow routes and check that planned services are carried out.

items.name: IoT sensors
items.text: Status and performance data from sensors on Cestò smart bins, roll-off containers and other company assets.

items.name: Citizen reports
items.text: Geo-referenced reports of issues across the city, managed by the control room from intake to resolution.

items.name: Base maps and satellite imagery
items.text: 2D and 3D maps of Rome with road network and service areas, plus satellite imagery used to detect illegal dumps.

deliverables: A live 2D/3D Digital Twin of Rome that shows reports, critical points and company assets on one map.
Operational dashboards with KPIs on service levels and criticalities, used to check that planned services are delivered.
Operating procedures that guide the control room from the intake of a report to the closure of the intervention.

methods.title: From raw data to the final product
text: The work starts with a technology assessment of AMA's existing systems, data sources and sensors, to see which data are available, how often they are updated and how they can be integrated. KPIs on service levels and criticalities are then defined, and the organisation is compared with other operations centres. On this basis, the target architecture of the Digital Twin and the process model of the control room are designed. Finally, dashboards are set up and procedures are defined to manage reports from receipt to closure.
